framework: Trade space for time with a hashmap/hashset to turn O(n^2) brute-force comparisons into O(n). Three recurring motifs: frequency counting (does this element repeat, how often), complement lookup (have I already seen the value I need to pair with this one), and grouping by a canonical key (e.g. sorted string or char-count signature for anagrams).
signal: Any 'have you seen this before', 'count occurrences', or 'group items that share a property' problem — usually your first instinct should be 'can a hashmap make this O(n)?'

framework: Opposite-direction pointers (start/end) close in toward each other for sorted-array target-sum and palindrome checks. Same-direction (fast/slow) pointers handle in-place array edits and linked-list cycle/middle detection.
signal: Sorted array + 'find a pair/triplet', or 'remove/dedupe in place', or linked-list cycle/middle.

framework: Expand a right pointer to grow the window until a condition is met or broken; shrink from the left while updating the best answer; maintain window state (hashmap/counter) incrementally, never recompute from scratch.
signal: 'Longest/shortest/count of substrings or subarrays satisfying X'.

framework: One unified while(left <= right) template. The only thing that changes between variants is what happens when nums[mid] == target: return immediately (exact match), keep shrinking right (find left boundary), or keep shrinking left (find right boundary). 'Search on the answer' reuses the exact same template over a value range instead of an index range.
signal: Sorted array, or a monotonic yes/no condition over a range of possible answers (capacity, speed, days).

framework: Use a dummy head node to remove edge-case branching at the list's start. Fast/slow pointers find the middle or detect a cycle (Floyd's). Reverse iteratively with prev/curr/next pointers, or recursively for reversing a sublist.
signal: Any 'reverse', 'find middle', 'detect/start of cycle', or 'merge k lists' problem.

framework: Keep a stack that is always increasing or always decreasing. Before pushing a new element, pop everything that violates monotonicity — each popped element just found its 'next greater/smaller' answer.
signal: 'Next greater/smaller element', daily temperatures, largest rectangle in histogram.

framework: Same idea as a monotonic stack but implemented as a deque, so you can pop from both ends — lets you maintain a sliding-window max/min in O(n) instead of O(n log n) with a heap.

Prefix sum array precomputes running totals so any range sum is one subtraction (O(1) per query). A difference array does the mirror trick for range *updates*: mark a delta at the start and end index, then reconstruct with one pass.
signal: Many range-sum queries on a static array, or many range-increment updates before a final read.

framework: For any tree problem, decide up front: is this a 'traversal' problem (visit every node, accumulate into external/instance state, like a manual for-loop) or a 'decompose' problem (define precisely what the recursive call on a subtree returns, then combine the children's results)? Default to the decompose framing — it generalizes to tree DP.
signal: Any binary tree problem, especially ones that feel like 'compute something about this subtree'.

framework: Level-order traversal with a queue and a visited set: for each level, pop everything currently in the queue, process it, and push unvisited neighbors — incrementing a step counter once per level, not per node.
signal: Shortest path / fewest steps in an unweighted graph or grid.

framework: Every backtracking problem shares one skeleton: track the current path (choices made), the list of remaining choices, and an end condition. Loop over choices -> make the choice -> recurse -> undo the choice. Subsets, combinations, permutations, and N-Queens are the same skeleton with different choice lists and pruning rules.
signal: 'Generate all ...' / 'find all valid ...' problems where brute force over choices is the only way in.

framework: Three-step framework: (1) identify the base case, (2) write a precise plain-English definition of what dp[i] / dp(i) means, (3) find the state-transition equation connecting dp[i] to smaller subproblems. Implement as top-down memoized recursion first (easier to reason about correctness), then convert to a bottom-up array if you need to strip recursion overhead.
signal: Overlapping subproblems + optimal substructure — ask 'what decision am I making at each step, and what do I need to remember about the past to make it?'

framework: At each step, make the locally optimal choice (often after sorting by some key — end time for interval scheduling, ratio for fractional knapsack) and trust — or prove — that local optimum compounds into a global optimum. Faster than DP whenever it's provably correct.
signal: Interval scheduling/merging, 'minimum number of X to cover Y', jump-game style reachability.

framework: Maintain a parent pointer per node; union() links two components' roots, find() walks to the root. Path compression + union-by-rank/size keep both operations near O(1) amortized.
signal: 'Are these connected?', dynamic connectivity as edges are added, cycle detection in an undirected graph.

framework: DFS/BFS generalize straight from trees to graphs — just add a visited set so you don't revisit nodes. Topological sort via Kahn's algorithm is BFS seeded from all zero-in-degree nodes (and doubles as a directed-cycle detector). Dijkstra is BFS with a min-heap priority queue instead of a plain queue, for weighted shortest paths.
signal: Course prerequisite / build-order problems (topo sort); weighted shortest path (Dijkstra); general graph connectivity/traversal.
